clue.text: TV comedy Addams Family’s final run? Could be

indicators.note: the final of a word is its closing letter, so only the end of Family is kept
the letters could be arranged otherwise, so the setter invites a rearrangement of what precedes

blocks.note: taken as written
the closing letter of Family
R is the cricket scorer's abbreviation for a run

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether a sitcom could be the last series of The Addams Family.
explanation.walkthrough: Dad's Army is a long-running BBC sitcom about the Home Guard in the Second World War; the 's is the possessive needed by both readings.
explanation.definitionFit: Dad's Army is a classic British television sitcom, so it is an example of a TV comedy.

clue.text: Following mother’s request, grew a plant

indicators.note: one piece following another means the later word is placed after the earlier ones

blocks.note: a dam is the mother of an animal, as in horse breeding
to ask is to request
rose is the past tense of rise, to grow

explanation.surface: Someone's plant grew after their mother asked them to look after it.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's of mother's is read as a possessive joining dam to ask; the last word comes first in the clue but last in the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The damask rose is a fragrant old garden rose cultivated for attar, so it is a particular plant.

clue.text: Study Old English houses

indicators.note: a phrase that houses something holds it inside, so the letters lie within the neighbouring words

blocks.note: found across the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: A scholar studies Old English in the houses where it was spoken.
explanation.definitionFit: A den is a small private room for reading or working, much like a study in a home.

clue.text: Don’t drink liqueur without the covering “Cheers!”

indicators.note: without means lacking, so the little word the is removed from the liqueur
something covering another goes round it, so the shortened liqueur wraps the toast

blocks.note: a green aniseed liqueur
taken as written, then removed
ta is informal British thanks, like cheers

explanation.surface: Advice to skip the liqueur, even when the whole table raises a glass and shouts cheers.
explanation.walkthrough: Absinthe is the green aniseed spirit; 'Cheers!' is the British thank-you, not a toast here, though the surface pulls toward drinking.
explanation.definitionFit: To abstain is to refrain voluntarily, especially from alcohol, so it fits a command not to drink.

clue.text: Doctor’s right first off, assuming Royal Society fellows may wear these

indicators.note: with its first off, the word loses its opening letter
to assume is to take on, so the society's initials take the shortened word inside them

blocks.note: MO is a medical officer
starboard is the right side of a ship
the usual initials of the Royal Society

explanation.surface: A medic suggests that Royal Society fellows may like to wear these when lined up on the right.
explanation.walkthrough: Right is the nautical side of a ship, not a direction or entitlement; the doctor is a medical officer, a common crossword abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: Mortarboards are square academic caps worn by university fellows and graduates at ceremonies.

clue.text: Clubs reportedly want people who’ll give a hand for pay

definitions.text: people who’ll give a hand for pay

indicators.note: reportedly means as heard spoken, so the result is a word that sounds the same

blocks.note: C is the abbreviation for clubs in card games
want in the sense of a shortage
the two pieces joined sound like the French borrowing

explanation.surface: A club wants hired people who will clap for money.
explanation.walkthrough: A claque is a group hired to applaud at a theatre; 'give a hand' means clap, not help.
explanation.definitionFit: A claque was a body of hired applauders paid to cheer performers in opera houses and theatres.

clue.text: Unrefined Neanderthal’s characteristic

blocks.note: first meaning: lacking cultural sophistication
second meaning: the sloping forehead typical of early humans

explanation.walkthrough: Neanderthal is also slang for a boor, so the second part seems to repeat the first; it is read literally as an anatomical feature.
explanation.definitionFit: Lowbrow describes uncultured taste, and literally a low forehead was the feature associated with Neanderthal skulls.

clue.text: Football player from, say, West Bromwich Albion covets Keegan’s caps

indicators.note: caps sit on top, so the heads of these words are taken

blocks.note: west is one of the four quarters of the compass, as say signals an example
the initial letter of each of these four words

explanation.surface: A West Bromwich Albion player envies the international caps won by Kevin Keegan.
explanation.walkthrough: West Bromwich Albion is a single English football club name, but West is split off; Kevin Keegan was an England captain with many caps.
explanation.definitionFit: A quarterback directs the offence in American football, so he is a kind of football player.

clue.text: Piece of cake making you nauseous, no question

indicators.note: no question means the abbreviation for question is taken away

blocks.note: feeling sick
QU is a standard abbreviation of question

explanation.surface: A slice of cake that unquestionably makes you feel sick.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Piece of cake' looks like food to be eaten, but it is the idiom for something simple.
explanation.definitionFit: A piece of cake is an idiom for something requiring no effort, which is what easy means.

clue.text: Skirts attempt to create government department

blocks.note: minis are short skirts
a try is an attempt

explanation.surface: Someone avoids an issue in an effort to set up a new government office.
explanation.walkthrough: Skirts reads as a verb meaning to avoid, but it is the plural noun for garments.
explanation.definitionFit: A ministry is a department of state headed by a minister, a branch of government.

clue.text: Pinches from vulnerable in backstreet

indicators.note: going back means running the abbreviation for street in the opposite direction
in places one piece inside another, here the weak word inside the street

blocks.note: weak means easily harmed
ST is the abbreviation for street, the word that follows back

explanation.surface: A thief steals from vulnerable people in a back alley.
explanation.walkthrough: Backstreet is read as two words: back reverses street. Pinches looks like stealing but means small twists.
explanation.definitionFit: A tweak is a sharp pinch or twist, so tweaks are pinches given to a nose or ear.

clue.text: Vehicle’s been pounded by officer with everyone detained? It’s way over our heads

indicators.note: something pounded is broken up, so its letters are rearranged
someone detained is held inside, so the word for everyone goes within the rest

blocks.note: a van is a vehicle
taken as written before rearranging
LT is the abbreviation for lieutenant
all means everyone

explanation.surface: A police van has been battered while an officer holds everyone in custody.
explanation.walkthrough: Everyone is held inside the whole string, just after the vehicle. 'Over our heads' sounds like something too hard to understand but is meant literally.
explanation.definitionFit: The Van Allen belts are zones of charged particles circling Earth high in space, far above everyone.

clue.text: In review, “Tosca lacks middle register ultimately, Scarpia’s OK” – so very disappointed

indicators.note: a word that lacks its middle keeps only its two ends
ultimately means at the end, so only the closing letter is kept
a review revisits material and reworks it, so the letters are reordered

blocks.note: the first and last letters of the opera's name
the closing letter of register
taken as written, the apostrophe ignored

explanation.surface: An opera critic finds the soprano weak in her middle register but rates the villain Scarpia's singing.
explanation.walkthrough: Tosca is Puccini's opera and Scarpia its villain, so the surface reads as a real review. 'Sick as a parrot' is a British football cliché for deep disappointment.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is British slang, famously used by footballers after defeat, for feeling bitterly let down.

clue.text: Nous sommes en Contes – half of that needs translating

indicators.note: only half of the last French word is wanted, so its second half is dropped
translating carries words into new form, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written before halving

explanation.surface: A French sentence about being in fairy tales, half of which needs translating into English.
explanation.walkthrough: Nous looks like the French word 'we', starting the French sentence, but it is the English word for practical intelligence.
explanation.definitionFit: In British usage nous is informal for practical good judgement, the same as plain sound sense.

clue.text: Bob, after tearing his hair out, will be so free from anxiety

blocks.note: a bob was an old British shilling, abbreviated S
a man who has torn out his hair is left with no locks

explanation.surface: A worried man named Bob will feel calm after tearing his hair out.
explanation.walkthrough: Bob looks like a man's name; it is slang for a shilling, the pre-decimal British coin written S. Tresses are locks of hair.
explanation.definitionFit: Stressless means without stress, untroubled by worry or strain, and so calm and relaxed.

clue.text: Novel’s an interminable book

indicators.note: interminable means without end, so the last letter of the book is dropped

blocks.note: Romans is a book of the New Testament

explanation.surface: A reader complains that a novel is a book that never ends.
explanation.definitionFit: Roman is the French word for a novel, used in English in terms such as roman à clef.

clue.text: 18’s wife brought in to explode banger in Munich?

indicators.note: brought in to means placed inside, so the pair goes within the word for explode

blocks.note: 18 down is a traitor, and a rat is a traitor
W is the abbreviation for wife
to burst is to explode

explanation.surface: A traitor's wife is brought in to set off a bomb in a German city.
explanation.walkthrough: Banger is British slang for a sausage, not an explosive; Munich hints that the sausage is German.
explanation.definitionFit: A bratwurst is a German pork sausage, so it is a banger as one might eat it in Bavaria.

clue.text: Insufficiency as result of early winter across the pond?

definitions.text: result of early winter across the pond?

blocks.note: first meaning: a deficit, an amount by which something falls below what is needed

blocks.clueFragment: result of early winter across the pond?
blocks.note: second meaning: in America autumn is fall, and an early winter cuts that season off

explanation.walkthrough: Across the pond means in America, where autumn is called the fall; winter arriving early leaves a short one.
explanation.definitionFit: A shortfall is a deficit or failure to reach a required amount, which is an insufficiency.

clue.text: Judas Priest’s last tour avoids university after unending strike

indicators.note: the last of a word is its final letter, so only the end of Priest is used
to avoid something is to leave it out, so the abbreviation for university is removed
without an ending, the word loses its final letter
after places the shortened tour behind the shortened strike

blocks.note: the final letter of Priest
an air raid is a strike
taken as written
U is the abbreviation for university

explanation.surface: Judas Priest, the heavy metal band, skip a university gig on their final tour after a strike.
explanation.walkthrough: Judas Priest is a British heavy metal band, but Judas is the definition and Priest supplies a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Judas Iscariot betrayed Jesus, so his name is used generically for any betrayer.

clue.text: Quench thirstiness at last with water

indicators.note: at last points to the final letter of the word before it

blocks.note: the final letter of thirstiness
a lake is a body of water

explanation.surface: At last someone satisfies their thirst with a drink of water.
explanation.definitionFit: To slake a thirst is to satisfy it, which is to quench it with a drink.

clue.text: Nice day? Bring lad round to visit

indicators.note: going round something means surrounding it, so the lad's word wraps the French day

blocks.note: a son is a lad
jour is French for day, as spoken in Nice

explanation.surface: On a pleasant day, someone brings a boy round to visit.
explanation.walkthrough: Nice is the French city, not the adjective, so the day is in French.
explanation.definitionFit: A sojourn is a temporary stay somewhere, a visit of some length.

clue.text: High jinks on stage entertaining duke – they always get a laugh

indicators.note: entertaining a guest means holding them within, so the abbreviation for duke goes inside
high in the sense of intoxicated suggests letters scrambled into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
D is the abbreviation for duke

explanation.surface: A duke is amused by high jinks on stage, comedy that always gets a laugh.
explanation.walkthrough: High jinks reads as one phrase meaning boisterous fun, but High is split off as the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Standing jokes are familiar recurring jokes that reliably raise laughs among those who share them.

clue.text: Children – that’s sons, not daughters – get smack

indicators.note: one abbreviation stands in place of another, sons replacing daughters

blocks.note: kids are children
D is the abbreviation for daughter
S is the abbreviation for son

explanation.surface: A parent says the boys, not the girls, get a smack.
explanation.walkthrough: Smack looks like punishment, but it is a loud kiss, as in a smacker.
explanation.definitionFit: A smack can be a loud kiss on the lips, so the two words share this sense.

clue.text: Make coal fire light first of all?

indicators.note: first of all picks out the opening letter of the word before it
the answer is what remains when a letter put at the front would make the fuel

blocks.note: lignite is soft brown coal
the opening letter of light

explanation.surface: A question about lighting a coal fire: do you need a flame first of all?
explanation.walkthrough: The clue works in reverse: putting L first on the answer would make lignite, a kind of coal.
explanation.definitionFit: To fire something is to set it alight, which is what ignite means as a verb.

clue.text: Embezzle money previously gathered by church collection

indicators.note: something gathered by another is held within it, so the money sits inside the collection

blocks.note: the collection plate passed round in church
the ecu was a European currency unit before the euro

explanation.surface: Someone steals the money that a church collection has gathered.
explanation.definitionFit: To peculate is to misappropriate funds entrusted to one, which is to embezzle them.

clue.text: Jana regularly pinches bottom of wing commander

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so every other letter of the name is taken
to pinch is to grip between two points, so the alternate letters close around another
the bottom of a down word is its last letter

blocks.note: the second and fourth letters
the final letter of wing

explanation.surface: A woman named Jana pinches a wing commander on the bottom.
explanation.walkthrough: Wing commander reads as one RAF rank, but wing is wordplay and commander alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An aga is a military commander or chief officer in the Ottoman Empire.

clue.text: Female takes Irishman with nothing out for a drink

indicators.note: with nothing out means the letter shaped like zero is removed

blocks.note: she is a female
Rory is a typical Irish name
O looks like a zero

explanation.surface: A woman takes an Irishman out for a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: Out reads as going out on a date, but it removes the O.
explanation.definitionFit: Sherry is a fortified wine from southern Spain, so it is a drink.

clue.text: Pupils from European country second to last

indicators.note: the second letter is taken out of its place and put to the end

blocks.note: a person from Estonia

explanation.surface: Schoolchildren from a European country come second to last in a contest.
explanation.walkthrough: Second to last looks like a ranking, but it is an instruction to move the second letter to the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Etonians are boys educated at Eton College, the English boarding school, so they are pupils.
